history.title: Energy Week

data.body:
**Due:** (your teacher will tell you)

Energy is not a thing you can hold. It is what lets one thing make something else happen. This week you follow it around.

1. Read **Energy Moves**.
2. Learn the words in **Energy Words**, then win the **Matching** game and the **Memory** game.
3. Study the **Four Ways Energy Travels** chart.
4. Sort the cards in **How Did It Travel?**
5. Practise explaining with **Energy Frames**, then check the rubric.
6. Take **Energy Check**.
7. Lock it in with **Remember Where It Went**.
8. Read **Energy Questions Kids Ask**.
9. Finish with **Design Challenge: Make Something Happen**.

Watch for one moment this week where energy clearly moved from one thing to another. ⚡

Picture panels: Compare movement; Follow a collision and a circuit; Track where energy goes; Light and sound in action. Pictures and arrows are models, not measurements. Repeated ball positions are successive observations, not multiple balls. Speed comparisons use the same mass and equal time intervals. Collision panels show an idealized equal-mass, straight-on case; actual results vary. Electric current means flow of charge, not energy itself. Heat flows spontaneously from warmer to cooler overall; powered heat pumps can transfer heat the other way. Energy is conserved while changing form and spreading out. Light cones, sound arcs and warmth wisps are illustrative conventions, not visible solid material. Sorting follows the specific journey named on each card, although devices can transfer energy in several ways. Appliance pictures are observation examples; practical circuit work uses teacher-approved low-voltage batteries. Do not handle hot liquids or household wiring for these activities.

history.title: Energy Moves
history.data:
## Energy Moves

You cannot hold **energy** in your hand. You cannot put it in a jar. But you can see what it does.

Energy is what lets one thing make something else happen. A moving ball knocks over a cup. A hot pan warms the soup. A battery lights a bulb. In each one, something changed, and energy is the reason.

### Faster means more

Anything moving has energy, and how much depends on its **speed**. Roll a ball slowly into a stack of blocks and one block wobbles. Roll the same ball fast and the whole stack scatters.

The ball did not get heavier. It got faster, and faster means more energy of **motion**. This is why running into someone hurts more than walking into them.

### Energy does not stay put

Here is the important part. Energy can move from one place to another. That move is called a **transfer**, and it happens in four ways you meet every day.

**Sound.** A drum is hit, the drum skin shakes, and the shaking travels through the air. When it reaches your ear, you hear it. If the drum is loud enough you feel it in your chest, because the energy really did travel to you.

**Light.** The Sun is very far away, and its energy still reaches your face. A torch sends energy across a dark room to the wall.

**Heat.** Put a metal spoon in hot soup and the handle warms up. The energy moved along the spoon, from the hot end toward the cool end. On its own, net heat transfer goes from warmer to cooler. A device such as a refrigerator needs an energy supply to move heat the other way.

**Electric current.** In a complete circuit, electric charge flows through the wires and bulb. This flow is called current. Energy transfers from the battery to the bulb, which glows.

### Crashes are transfers

When two things **collide**, energy moves between them. In a nearly elastic, straight-on collision between equal-mass marbles, the rolling marble can nearly stop while the still marble moves away. Real results depend on the objects and the collision. The energy went from the first to the second.

Some of it usually leaks out too. A collision often makes a sound, and the objects can get slightly warmer. That sound and that warmth are energy, leaving in another form.

### It never just vanishes

People say energy gets used up. It does not. It **changes** form and it spreads out.

A torch does not destroy the energy in its battery. It turns it into light and a little heat. A bouncing ball ends up still on the floor, and the energy went into sound and warming the ground very slightly.

So when something stops happening, do not ask where the energy went missing. Ask where it went. There is always an answer.

data.title: Remember Where It Went
data.instructions: Two cards hold the ideas you will use all week. Read the example, then make one of your own and say why it works.
data.sourceExcerpt: People say energy gets used up. It does not. It changes form and it spreads out. A torch does not destroy the energy in its battery. It turns it into light and a little heat.

cards.target: The four ways energy travels from place to place
essentialFacts: Sound travels as shaking through the air.
Light travels in straight lines and crosses empty space.
Heat moves from a warmer thing to a cooler one.
An electric current carries energy along a wire.
cards.aiExample: Picture one room with four things in it. A drum on the floor. A lamp on the table. A mug of tea beside it. A plug in the wall. Sound, light, heat, current. One room holds all four ways.
cards.mapping: One picture instead of a list of four, and each object is something you have actually stood next to, so recalling the room recalls the four.
scaffoldSteps: Picture a room you know well.
Find one object for each of the four ways.
Say what is transferring energy in each one.
coachPrompts: Which of the four is hardest to spot in your room?
cards.studentPrompt: Build your own room with all four ways in it.
cards.reasoningPrompt: Could one object show two ways at once? Give an example.

hookFact.text: If the drum is loud enough you feel it in your chest, because the energy really did travel to you.

cards.target: Energy never vanishes, so always ask where it went
essentialFacts: Energy changes form and spreads out.
A torch turns battery energy into light and a little heat.
A collision often makes sound and a little warmth.
cards.aiExample: Ask two questions in this order, every time. WHERE FROM? WHERE TO? The ball stopped rolling. Where from: the ball moving. Where to: sound and a slightly warmer floor.
cards.mapping: Two questions in a fixed order turn a vague thought into a trail you can actually follow, and the second one stops you from saying the energy just disappeared.
scaffoldSteps: Name something that stopped or changed.
Ask where the energy came from.
Ask where it went, and name a form.
coachPrompts: You said it stopped. Where did the energy go?

history.title: Energy Frames
history.meta: 6 frames • say them out loud before writing • rubric included

items.text: The energy started in ____ and ended up in ____.
It travelled as ____, and I know because ____.
When ____ moved faster, ____ happened, which shows it had more energy.
When ____ and ____ collided, the energy moved from ____ to ____.
Some energy also left as ____, which is why ____.
It did not get used up. It changed into ____.

data.rubric:
| Criteria | 1 — Starting | 3 — Getting There | 5 — Explaining |
|---|---|---|---|
| Following the energy | Says something happened | Names where the energy started | Names where it started AND where it ended up |
| Naming the way | Not named | Names sound, light, heat or current | Names it and gives the observation that shows it |
| Nothing vanishes | Says the energy was used up | Says it changed | Names the new form, including energy that left as sound or warmth |

history.title: Energy Check

questions.question: You roll the same ball faster into a stack of blocks. What happens, and why?
options: The stack scatters more, because faster means more energy
The stack scatters more, because the ball became heavier
The stack barely moves, because speed does not affect energy
The stack moves the same amount, because it is the same ball
questions.correctAnswer: The stack scatters more, because faster means more energy

questions.question: A metal spoon in hot soup gets warm. Which way did the energy travel?
options: From the cool handle down into the hot soup
From the hot soup up along the spoon to the handle
It did not travel; the handle made its own heat
It travelled as light along the shiny metal
questions.correctAnswer: From the hot soup up along the spoon to the handle

questions.question: Which way does net heat flow on its own?
options: From a cooler thing to a warmer thing
Toward whichever thing is bigger
From a warmer thing to a cooler thing
Downward, because heat is heavy
questions.correctAnswer: From a warmer thing to a cooler thing

questions.question: A rolling marble hits a still marble and stops. What happened to its energy?
options: It was destroyed the moment the marble stopped
It stayed inside the first marble but went quiet
It turned into extra weight in the second marble
It transferred to the second marble, which moved away
questions.correctAnswer: It transferred to the second marble, which moved away

questions.question: A bouncing ball finally lies still on the floor. What is the best explanation?
options: The energy changed into sound and slight warming
The energy was used up completely and is now gone
The energy sank down into the ground and stopped there
The ball never really had any energy to begin with
questions.correctAnswer: The energy changed into sound and slight warming

questions.question: What does a torch actually do with the energy from its battery?
options: It destroys that energy in order to make brightness
It changes that energy into light and a little heat
It stores the energy up until the battery is empty
It moves the energy into the air around the torch
questions.correctAnswer: It changes that energy into light and a little heat

questions.question: You clap your hands. Follow the energy: where did it start, and where did it end up?
questions.expectedAnswer: It started as energy of the moving hands. During the clap, some energy transferred to the air as sound and some became thermal energy in the hands and surroundings. The proportions are not measured here. Energy was transferred and transformed, not destroyed.

questions.question: A friend says a battery gets used up because the energy inside it is destroyed. What would you tell them?
questions.expectedAnswer: Energy is not destroyed. As a battery powers a device, stored chemical energy transfers and changes into other forms, such as light and thermal energy. A flat battery can no longer supply enough electrical energy for that device under those conditions.

history.title: Energy Questions Kids Ask

data.question: If energy never vanishes, why do batteries go flat? 🔋
data.answer: As a battery powers a device, stored chemical energy is transferred and changed into forms such as light, sound and thermal energy. A flat battery can no longer supply enough electrical energy for the device. The transferred energy still exists, often dispersed as thermal energy that is less useful for doing the original job.

data.question: Is energy a thing or an idea? 🤔
data.answer: A bit of both, and scientists argue about how to say it. It is not stuff you can collect in a bucket. It is more like an amount that things have, and the useful part is that the amount can be tracked as it moves.

data.question: Can energy travel through empty space?
data.answer: Light can, which is how sunlight crosses space to reach us. Sound cannot, because sound needs something to shake. Space is silent.

data.question: Where does the energy in food come from? 🌱
data.answer: From the Sun, by a longer path than you might expect. Plants capture sunlight, animals eat plants, and we eat both. Almost all the energy in your lunch started as sunlight.

data.question: Does a still object have any energy at all?
data.answer: It has no energy of motion, since it is not moving. But it can still hold energy in other ways, such as a stretched rubber band or a book resting on a high shelf. Let either one go and you will see it.

data.question: Why do my hands warm up when I rub them? 🙌
data.answer: You are moving them, and rubbing turns some of that motion into heat. It is the same reason a slide feels warm after you go down it fast.

history.title: Design Challenge: Make Something Happen
history.meta: 4th Grade • Design brief • build a device that changes energy from one form to another

data.title: Make Something Happen
data.instructions: Build something that takes energy in one form and turns it into another. Test it, improve it once, and trace where the energy goes.
data.fitReason: Energy conversion stays abstract until a student builds a thing that does it and has to say what became what. Requiring one round of improvement is what makes it engineering rather than craft, and tracing the leaks is where the never-vanishes rule stops being a slogan.

brief.context: You will have simple materials: card, string, tape, rubber bands, marbles, paper cups, straws, a torch, a small ramp. Your teacher may add batteries, wires and bulbs. Everything must be safe to hold and drop.
brief.audience: The class, who will try each device and try to say what turned into what
brief.drivingQuestion: What went in, what came out, and where did the rest of it go?
brief.seedDirection: Start with motion, because it is the easiest form to make and the easiest to see. A ramp and a marble is enough to begin.
lockedLessonFacts: For the same mass, faster motion means more kinetic energy.
Energy transfers by sound, light, heat and electric currents.
When two things collide, energy moves between them.
Energy changes form and spreads out; it never just vanishes.
openQuestions: What happened when you made the starting motion faster?
Where did energy leak out that you did not plan for?
Could someone watching tell what turned into what, without you explaining?
stakeholders: A classmate who has to work out how your device runs
Your partner, who tests it while you watch
A younger student who might build it next year
criteria: Your device turns energy from one form into another
You name what went in and what came out
You test it twice, change one thing, and say what happened
You name one place energy leaked out, such as sound or warmth
constraints: Nothing that could hurt anyone if it went wrong
It has to fit on a desk
Change only one thing between the two tests
brief.deliverable: Your working device, plus a short card showing what went in, what came out, one place energy leaked, and what changed between your two tests.

parallelExample.context: A student built a ramp so a marble rolled down and knocked a paper cup off the desk edge.
parallelExample.move: The first run barely nudged the cup. He raised the ramp so the marble arrived faster, and the second run sent the cup flying. On his card he wrote that motion went in, motion came out, and some energy left as the click he could hear at the moment of the hit.
parallelExample.whyItHelps: Changing only the ramp height meant he could say exactly why the second run worked better. Noticing the click is what showed he understood that leaks are energy too, not just noise.

What did you hear or feel that you did not plan for?
What is the one thing you changed between your two tests?
